name: Sara Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an overhead crew in the city, in the old Eastgate neighbourhoods where the poles are squeezed into back lanes between garages and washing lines. We replace old transformers, fix broken service wires, and untangle the mess people have made over fifty years. I'm a first-year apprentice, so I'm on the ground: traffic control, passing tools up on the hand line, keeping nosy children away from the truck. We leave the depot at seven, and by eight I've usually had two grandmothers ask me if I'm really a lineman. I love that the job is real, it's for families; what wears me out is my shoulders and the radio in the truck, always news.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it at your age?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I raised five children, and for fifteen years I was the part-time secretary and bookkeeper at our church. When the youngest left home, I thought, Lord, what now? My nephew is a lineworker and he said they were short of apprentices and didn't care about age if you could pass the tests. Samuel, my husband, drives a city bus, and with five children through school and two weddings, there's never more than a few weeks of money in the bank. I use AI every day, for my studies, the church rota, even helping my mother read her letters, and the young men on the crew can't believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still a good tool, even if it's not a miracle. At work I'd keep showing the boys how I use it to study. At church I'd say God gave us brains to make tools, and this is just another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes much, and that's fine. I'm still learning the trade and still using AI to help me study. If anything I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped it would make life easier for people like my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my apprenticeship and keep studying with AI for my exams. I'd keep doing the church books on Saturdays, which brings in a little. I'd try to save a hundred a month, which Samuel and I have promised each other every year since our first child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really, though a little disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the young men on the crew can't believe it. What do they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darnell, who's twenty-four, said, Miss Sara, how do you know more about this than me? I told him I had five teenagers once, so I learned every gadget just to keep up with what they were doing. Now he asks me to explain the theory questions it gives me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A hundred a month every year since your first child. What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Life. School shoes, a wedding, a funeral back home, a car repair, a son who needed help with rent for three months. I don't regret any of it, family comes first, but it means at fifty-eight I've got about three weeks of money saved, and that worries me more than any robot.

S0.say: AI is still a good tool, even if it's not a miracle. At church she would say God gave people brains to make tools, and this is just another one.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for her: she keeps learning and studying with AI. She'd be a bit disappointed, having hoped it would make life easier for people like her mother.
S0.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship and studies with AI for her exams. Keeps doing the church books on Saturdays for a little extra and tries again to save a hundred a month.
S0.feel: Calm and content, with a little disappointment.
S0.quote: I told him I had five teenagers once, so I learned every gadget just to keep up with what they were doing.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is a confident, curious AI user with deep roots in family and church. Her thin savings come from years of putting family first, which she doesn't regret. Her money worries outweigh any fear of technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity, if people are willing to work and learn. At work I'd tell the boys to learn the tools now. At church I'd say we should help each other through it, the way families and churches always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I'm slow up the pole, but I'm quick with the tablet and the AI, and if the job changes toward smart grid work and drones, I'll be ready. City crews will still need people for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for any pilot project the company runs with new tools, in the first month. I'd start teaching a small class at church on Saturday afternoons for older people who want to learn AI, maybe charge a little. I'd help my youngest, Joseph, choose his course at college with all this in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. It feels like God's timing, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help Joseph choose his course. What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to do business studies, and I'd tell him to add something practical, like electrical or plumbing, so he has a trade under him. Business is good, but a business that knows how to fix things is better. He'd say, Mum, you sound like Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You seem very positive. Is there anything about this one that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young men on the crew who don't want to learn. Darnell's fine, but Marcus refuses to touch the tablet, and he's got two babies at home. I'd worry about him, and I'd try to help him without making him feel small.

S1.say: This is an opportunity for people willing to work and learn. At church she would say families and churches should help each other through it, as they always have.
S1.think: She thinks it's good for her, since she's quick with technology even if slow up the pole. City crews will still need people for years.
S1.do: Volunteers for company pilot projects with new tools in the first month and starts a small paid Saturday class at church teaching older people to use AI. Helps her youngest son choose a college course with a practical trade.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like it's God's timing.
S1.quote: Business is good, but a business that knows how to fix things is better.
S1.fieldNote: Sara sees steady change as an opportunity that fits both her skills and her faith. She immediately thinks of side income and of helping her son choose wisely. Her concern for a younger colleague who refuses new tools shows a caring, practical streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, but we'll get through it with faith and family. At work I'd tell the boys to stay calm and learn what they can. I'd want the government to support apprenticeships for the new work, not just send out cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty, with barely any savings and just about qualified. If robots can climb poles by 2028, even my AI skills might not be enough, because the AI won't need me to explain it. I'd still try, but I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company straight away to train me on the robots and the systems that run them, because someone has to supervise them. I'd grow the AI class at church into a proper small business, teaching or helping people with forms and bookkeeping. And we'd cut back at home, no visits back home this year, no extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for sure. But I don't feel hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said faith and family. What would family actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five children, and three of them doing well, so if Samuel and I needed help with the rent for a few months, they'd help. We helped them, so they'd help us, that's how it's supposed to work. I'd hate it, but I'd accept it before I'd go to the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years give you, compared to more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just enough to get a foot in the door of the new work, if I move first. I've watched people wait and lose out before, at the church when the money got tight. So I'd move first, and I'd pray hard.

S2.say: It's too fast, but faith and family will get people through. She would want the government to support apprenticeships for new work rather than send cheques.
S2.think: At sixty, barely qualified and with little savings, even her AI skills might not be enough when the AI doesn't need explaining. She would still try, but she'd be worried.
S2.do: Asks immediately to be trained on supervising robots and the systems that run them. Grows her church AI class into a small business helping people with forms and bookkeeping, and cuts back at home.
S2.quote: If robots can climb poles by 2028, even my AI skills might not be enough, because the AI won't need me to explain it.
S2.fieldNote: Sara's confidence is shaken but not broken in the fast scenario. Her fallback is family, which she prefers over government help, and her instinct is to move first. She sees a business opportunity even in a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to prepare, if people start now. At work I'd push the boys to get trained on new kit. At church I'd say let's help each other get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three, qualified and experienced with the new tools. I think I could carve out a role supervising the robots, or helping train people. It's not much time to save, but it's enough to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship by 2029 and take any course on the new systems. I'd build up the AI teaching and bookkeeping business to bring in a few hundred a month. I'd save that money, because that's my cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly I'd feel busy and useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A few hundred a month from a side business. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. There are a lot of older people at our church and in Eastgate who are frightened of these things and can't afford to pay much. If I charge a little and do it well, word gets around, and I already do the church books so people trust me with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Samuel say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, Sara, you're doing too much, and he'd be right. But then he'd help me set up the chairs on Saturday afternoon. He's been driving buses for thirty years, and he's worried about the self-driving buses, so I'd want to bring him into the business too.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to prepare if people start now. She would push crewmates to train on new equipment and her church to help one another get ready.
S3.think: At sixty-three, qualified and experienced with new tools, she thinks she could carve out a role supervising robots or training people. Five years isn't much time to save, but enough to get ready.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship by 2029 and takes courses on new systems. Builds her AI teaching and bookkeeping business to a few hundred a month and saves it as her cushion.
S3.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly busy and useful.
S3.quote: There are a lot of older people at our church and in Eastgate who are frightened of these things and can't afford to pay much.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Sara has a clear plan combining her trade with a side business built on trust from her church role. She is realistic about time and money. Her husband's worry about self-driving buses gives her another reason to grow the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no one has an excuse. At work I'd say let's all get ready. At church I'd say this is a chance to help people, especially the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, probably retired from the lines. With the side business and some savings, I think I'd be fine. My worry would be for my children and grandchildren, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship, work on the lines as long as I'm useful, and build the side business slowly. I'd save a bit every month. I'd sit down with each of my five children and talk about their work and what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel ready, and I'd want to help others get ready too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five conversations with five children. Which one worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My eldest, Grace, who works in a bank call centre. That's the first kind of work AI takes, and she's got three children. I'd tell her to start learning something else now, maybe nursing, because people will always want a person at the bedside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been calm throughout. Is there anything you're afraid of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being useless. Not poor, I've been poor, but useless. If there's no work for anyone, I'd still want to be the one at church who helps people fill in forms or learn the new things, because a person needs to be needed.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so no one has an excuse. At church she would call it a chance to help people, especially the young.
S4.think: At sixty-eight she would probably be retired from the lines, and with a side business and some savings she thinks she'd be fine. Her worry is for her children and grandchildren.
S4.do: Finishes her apprenticeship, works on the lines while useful and builds her side business slowly. Saves monthly and sits down with each of her five children to talk about their work and the future.
S4.feel: Calm and ready, wanting to help others get ready too.
S4.quote: Not poor, I've been poor, but useless.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sara feels calm and ready, and her focus turns to her children, especially her eldest in a bank call centre. Her deepest fear is not poverty but being useless. Her sense of purpose comes from helping others through church.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there'd be no time to save or build anything. What would help is training for older workers on the new systems, and support for small businesses like the one I'd start. Help people stand on their own feet, not hand them money and walk away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like being a woman my age on a line crew. The first week, a man on the street asked me if I was the crew's mother. I said, today I'm the one holding the rope that keeps your power on.

headlineQuote: I said, today I'm the one holding the rope that keeps your power on.
portrait: Sara Okafor is a 58-year-old first-year apprentice on a city overhead crew in Eastgate, who joined after raising five children and working as her church's part-time secretary and bookkeeper. She and her husband Samuel, a bus driver, have only a few weeks of savings after years of putting family first. She uses AI every day and sees steady change as an opportunity, planning a small business teaching older people to use AI. The 2028 picture makes her anxious but not hopeless, and she would lean on her children before the government. With more time she feels ready and turns her worry to her children's jobs.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because there would be no time to save or build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Training for older workers on the new systems and support for small businesses, helping people stand on their own feet rather than handing them money.
